column2: One whose brows are not joined or crooked, whose life is her husband and who is dear to her husband — even without marks she is auspicious; where there are such forms, there are virtues.
She whose little finger does not touch the ground — death itself.
It should be three cubits in breadth, painted with gold and the like. A bow has three materials: iron, horn, wood, best of twice-born;
the bow-string has three materials: bamboo-fiber, bark and the like. The best wooden bow is four cubits in measure;
that same measure reduced is told for the middling and lowest. One should make in the middle the materials for the grip of the fist;
with a small tip, of bark, horn, or of shārnga-iron, twice-born; the tip should be made well joined, like a woman's brow-vine.
Separately or mixed, Brahmin, one should make the iron shārnga; the shārnga should be made suitably, adorned with gold dots.
A crooked, cracked or holed bow is not praised. Gold, silver, copper and black iron are remembered for a bow;
a bow of buffalo horn, sharabha horn, shārnga or rohisha is auspicious; sandal, cane, sala, dhava, arjuna wood;
the best of all is a bow of bamboos taken and settled in autumn. One should worship bow and sword with the mantras that bewilder the three worlds.
Of iron or bamboo, arrow or non-arrow, the priests of the golden hue, bound with sinew, with good feathers,
with golden shafts, well-muddled, oil-washed, golden — at a journey, consecration and the like the king should worship arrows and bows,
with banners, the weapon-takers and the astrologers. Brahma once sacrificed on the peak of Meru on the bank of the heavenly Ganga;
thinking of an obstacle in the sacrifice he saw an iron demon; as he thought, from the fire a great strong person arose.
He saluted the Unborn, and the gods rejoiced and welcomed him; therefore he, named Nandaka, the sword told by the gods, Hari took.
The god slowly took him; he became the sword without a sheath: blue, with jewelled hilt; then he became hundred-armed.
That demon with a mace routed the gods in battle. By Vishnu's sword the demon's limbs were cut and fell on the ground,
and by Nandaka's touch they all became iron. Having killed him, Hari gave him a boon:
May your body be a pure weapon on earth. By Hari's grace Brahma, without obstacle, worshipped Hari the Lord
with sacrifice. Now I shall tell the marks of a sword. Those born of khati and khattara are said to be to be seen;
those of Tvashika are body-cutting, firm, those of Surparaka; sharp, enduring cutting are the Vanga ones; sharp are those born in Anga;
a sword of fifty fingers is declared the best; half of that is to be known as middling; less than that one should not bear.
A sword whose sound is long and very sweet, like a small bell — carrying it is said to be best.
A sword with a tip like a lotus petal and a round tip is praised; with tip like an oleander leaf, scented like ghee, shining like the sky;
wounds on swords standing at equal fingers are praised, like a mark; those colored like crow or owl are uneven and not good.
One should not look at one's face in a sword; an unclean one should not touch a sword; one should not tell its price or origin; one should not keep it at the head at night.
Serpent-gem and diamond-gem are auspicious, tittibha, pinda, bhramara and utpala (gems);
gems bound in gold bring prosperity and victory. Inner luster, purity and good shape;
those without luster, dirty, broken or gritty should not be worn; wearing a diamond is praised.
A diamond that floats on water, unbreakable and spotless, six-cornered, rainbow-colored, light and sun-like, is auspicious.
An emerald resembling a parrot's wing, glossy, lustrous and spotless, with fine dots like gold dust, is good.
Rubies are crystal-born, colored and very clear; born of vanga here, born of kuruvinda;
born of saugandhika, kashaya (tinted); pearls are oyster-born; spotless ones are better; those conch-born, sage,
born of elephant tusks are chief; born of pot, boar and fish; born of bamboo and serpent are best; the cloud-born pearl is best.
Roundness, whiteness, clarity and size are the qualities in a pearl. A sapphire in milk is auspicious, in silver it shines more;
it colors by its own power: declare it priceless. A blue-red cat's-eye is best; one should use it in necklaces and the like.
Pavana in the east; Antariksha and Dhaneshvara; in the southeast and southwest the gods Mriga and Sugriva;
Roga and Mukhya in the northwest; in the south Pushpa and Vittada; Grihakshata, Yama and Bhrisha, Gandharva, Naga and Pitrika;
in the west Dauvarika and Sugriva, Pushpadanta, Asura, Jala; Yakshma, Roga and Shosha in the north; Nagaraja;
Mukhya, Bhallata and Shashin, Aditi and Kubera; Naga, Hutasha the best, and Shakra and Surya in the east;
in the south Grihakshata, Pushpa; in the west Sugriva best; Pushpadanta in the north door; Bhallata, Pushpadanta.
Having worshipped the gods with mantras one should perform the setting of stones, bricks and the like: "O Nanda, delight, daughter of Vasishtha, with wealth and offspring;
Jaya, daughter of Bhargava, victory for the subjects in battle; Purna, daughter of Angiras, fulfil my desire;
Bhadra, daughter of Kashyapa, make my mind auspicious; joined with all seeds, surrounded by all jewels and herbs,
lovely, delighting Nanda, daughter of Vasishtha, be pleased here; daughter of Prajapati, goddess, four-cornered, made of earth,
fortunate, well-vowed Bhadra, daughter of Kashyapa, be pleased in the house; worshipped by great teachers, adorned with scents and garlands,
making prosperity, goddess, Bhargavi, be pleased in the house; unbroken, unspoiled, full, daughter of the sage Angiras,
brick, grant what is wished; I establish you; in the possession of the lord of the country, of the city and of the house,
be the increaser of people, wealth, elephants, horses and cattle." Also at house-entry one should perform the laying of the stone.
To the north a plaksha is auspicious; a banyan to the east of the house; an udumbara to the south; in the west a pipal is best;
on the left a garden should be made; dwelling is good in the house. Planted trees should be watered evening and morning in heat, in cold season by day's end,
in rainy nights and especially in drought; one should water them with cold water mixed with vidanga and ghee.
When fruit is lost, with kulattha, masha, mudga, sesame and barley; a sprinkling of ghee and cool milk gives fruit and flowers always.
By sprinkling with fish-water the tree grows. Sheep-and-goat dung powder, barley powder, sesame,
cow-flesh and water — one should keep these for seven nights; this sprinkling for all trees increases fruit, flowers and the like.
For mangoes, sprinkling with cool fish-water is desired. For ashokas the stroke of a woman's foot is praised;
for date palms, coconut and the like, growth by salt water; vidanga, fish and flesh in water — a longing-wish is auspicious for all.
Ashoka, tilaka, kunda are for worship; the tamala-born; bilva leaf, shami leaf, and the leaf of bhringaraja;
tulasi and black tulasi leaf, vasaka in worship; leaf and flower of ketaki, and lotus, red lotus and the like;
not arka, not unmatta, not kankanchi in worship; girimallika; kutaja and shalmali flowers; not what is born of kantakari.
Bathing Vishnu with a prastha of ghee has the fine fruit of a crore of cows; with an adhaka one becomes a king; by ghee and milk one goes to heaven.
What is thrown by a machine, such as a bow-machine, is called yantra-mukta; stone, javelin machines and the like are called pani-mukta;
mukta-sandharita is to be known, also what would be a lance and the like; sword and the like is amukta; wrestling is weaponless.
One wishing to fight, having conquered fatigue, should make suitable vessels. Bow-wars are best, spear-wars middling;
sword-wars lowest, and arm-wars the least. In the science of archery the teacher is a Brahmin, said for two castes;
the Shudra's right to fight is by himself, by training. The king's help in battle should be made by the mixed castes living in the country.
If thumb, ankle, hand and foot are joined together, that is the "samapada" stance, seen thus by marks;
where both knees are seen shaped like a row of swans, separated by four spans, that is remembered as "mandala";
shaped like a plough, with the right knee and thigh stiff, five spans in breadth, that is called "alidha";
the very reverse is remembered as "pratyalidha." The left should be oblique and the right straight;
ankles and heels set five fingers apart — this arisen stance is twelve fingers long;
the left knee straight and the right well extended; or the right knee bent and motionless;
this foot together with the knee should be staff-long: thus "vikata" is taught, two hands apart in length;
the knees doubled and both feet supine: by this method "samputa" is declared;
feet slightly turned, equal, staff-long, steady; seen as it should be, sixteen fingers long.
